name: Communism, after Saigon
also: what happened after the war; where the idea went next; what became of every nation that defended Saigon and withdrew
premise: Full stop on Saigon. The rooms end there. This page begins there: the Americans left, every nation that had contributed to the funded war effort in the defence of Saigon withdrew with them, and then communism — the thing the whole manner of resistance had been built to contain — went on, both in Vietnam and in the world, until it did not.
vietnam: Re-education: about 200,000–300,000 former ARVN officers, officials and professionals sent to camps; some for months, some for seventeen years.
Laos: the monarchy abolished; the Pathet Lao take the state without a battle. The Hmong who fought for the CIA are hunted for a decade.
Reunification: the Socialist Republic of Vietnam; Saigon renamed; collectivisation in the South begins and fails.
Cambodia: the Khmer Rouge empty the cities on the first day and kill 1.5–2 million of 8 million in four years.
Vietnam invades Cambodia and ends the Khmer Rouge in two weeks; the world, including the United States and China, keeps recognising the Khmer Rouge at the UN until 1991.
China invades Vietnam to punish it for Cambodia; a month, tens of thousands dead on each side; two communist states at war, which the domino theory had not allowed for.
The boat people: about 800,000 reach other shores; perhaps 200,000–400,000 do not. The Orderly Departure Program from 1979; the refugees resettle in the United States, Australia, Canada, France.
Doi Moi, renovation: the party keeps the state and gives up the economy. Vietnam becomes a market with a politburo.

The US embargo lifted; 1995-07, diplomatic relations; 2000, Clinton in Hanoi; 2016, the arms embargo lifted; 2023, a comprehensive strategic partnership. Vietnam is now, by treaty, a partner of the nation it defeated, against the neighbour that armed it.
The party rules. The camps are closed. The Wall in Washington has 58,000 names and Vietnam has no wall, and the toll on its side is still a range, not a number.

contributors.after: The draft ended; the War Powers Resolution; the Weinberger–Powell doctrine; the “Vietnam syndrome” declared over in 1991 and not over. Normalised relations 1995.
Came home to a dictatorship it had fought for abroad; democracy in 1987; the Korean veterans’ Agent Orange claims recognised in the 1990s; now the largest foreign investor in Vietnam.
Ended conscription the same week; recognised Hanoi in 1973; took 200,000 Vietnamese refugees over the next decades, the beginning of the end of White Australia.
The veterans got an apology from Parliament in 2008 for how they were received.
Held the line the dominoes were supposed to cross: a communist insurgency in the northeast peaked in the late 1970s and was amnestied away by 1983; took in a million refugees from three countries.
Marcos’s martial law in 1972; the New People’s Army, a communist insurgency, still in the field fifty years later.
Lost the American recognition to Beijing in 1979, four years after Saigon.
The two dominoes that fell. Cambodia’s fall killed a quarter of its people; Laos is still a one-party state.
Kept its embassy in Hanoi throughout, and its schools in Saigon to the end.

spread.unit: States governed by a communist party, by year (approximate)

next: Angola: the MPLA, with Cuban troops; a proxy war for sixteen years.
Afghanistan: the Saur coup; the Soviet invasion in December 1979; the American answer through the mujahideen, the war after this war.
Nicaragua: the Sandinistas; the contras; the Boland amendments, written by the Congress that had learned from Vietnam; Iran–Contra, the executive learning nothing.
Grenada: the New Jewel Movement; the American invasion of October 1983, the first ground war after Vietnam, four days long, chosen for the length.
Poland: Solidarity — the first crack from inside.
Tiananmen; and the same month Poland votes; November, the Wall.
The Soviet Union dissolves. Of the twenty-five, five remain: China, Vietnam, Laos, Cuba, North Korea — three of them the parties to this war.

The five are still five. Two of them, China and Vietnam, are the world’s factory and its fastest-growing partner respectively, and each other’s adversary. The idea outlived its containment by being, in the end, less contained than adapted.
neighbours: Neighbours are not harbours. Every nation on the contributors’ list was a neighbour of the war before it was a party to it, and every one that took refugees afterward became a harbour by choice rather than by geography. The exception is the rule’s proof: Cambodia and Laos, the nearest neighbours, could be neither, and were taken. In the ledger this repository keeps, that is the difference between a syndicate that can audit its neighbour and one that can only be carried across by it.

text: After Saigon: the re-education camps, the boat people, the two communist wars of 1978–79, Doi Moi, the partnership with the enemy; what became of every nation that defended Saigon and withdrew; and where communism went next, from Angola to the Wall to the five that remain.
